newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Pope sends handover blessing to HK, China Catholics.
newsitem.headline: Pope sends handover blessing to HK, China Catholics.

text.p: Pope John Paul has sent a blessing to Hong Kong and Chinese Catholics, wishing them well for the British-ruled territory's handover to China next week, church leaders said on Friday.
And Hong Kong's Roman Catholic Church will attend the investiture of a controversial unelected legislature next Tuesday despite its opposition to the assembly, they said.

The Pope sent blessings in a letter to Hong Kong prelate, Cardinal John Baptist Wu, declaring: "I am close in prayer to your eminence, to the bishops, the clergy...and the entire diocesan community, as well as to all people of goodwill."
"My thoughts also go to the Catholics of mainland China, who at this time are united in a particular way with their brothers and sisters in the faith living in Hong Kong," the Pope said.

Bishop Joseph Zen told Reuters the Church had been invited and would attend the swearing-in ceremony of the new Hong Kong government hours after Britain hands the territory back to China, ending 156 years of colonial rule.

But, echoing concern by the West and pro-democracy campaigners here, he said the Church had reservations about the unelected interim legislature, to replace the elected parliament at midnight on Monday (1600 GMT).
"We have reservations about it because it is not in accordance to the will of the Hong Kong people," he said.
"It is not an elected body," Zen said. "We hope an election will be held as soon as possible," the bishop said.
Cardinal Wu, Bishop John Tong and Zen will represent the Church at the ceremony, Zen said.
British Prime Minister Tony Blair and U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright will boycott the swearing-in ceremony, but London and Washington will send senior envoys along.
Late last month, Zen and two top clerics made an undisclosed visit to China to discuss the Catholic Church's future under the rule of atheist Communist Chinese leaders.
They said their frank and friendly talks had "strengthened our confidence".
China has promised to respect religion, among other aspects of Hong Kong's way of life, for 50 years.
But some leaders of various faiths have expressed unease about civil liberties in the future.
Hong Kong has about 250,000 Catholics in a population of 6.4 million, nearly all Chinese.
Hong Kong's Catholic Church will hold a Mass on July 1 to mark the territory's return to China.
The Beijing government does not recognise the ultimate authority of the Vatican in religious affairs.
It insists Chinese Catholics worship under the auspices of a state-controlled Catholic Patriotic Association.
